questions.title: Explain double-slit interference
questions.prompt: Two narrow slits are illuminated by coherent monochromatic light of wavelength 500 nm. The waves leave the slits in phase and have equal amplitudes at the screen points considered. At P, the two paths differ by 1000 nm. At Q, they differ by 750 nm. Use the path differences to predict the fringes.

parts.prompt: Determine the path difference at P in wavelengths.

options.feedback: 1000/500 is 2, not one half.
1000 nm contains two wavelengths of 500 nm.
1000/500 = 2 wavelengths.
Divide by 500 nm to count the wavelengths.

parts.correctFeedback: 1000/500 = 2 wavelengths.

options.feedback: Constructive superposition reinforces the waves, so the fringe is bright.
A bright fringe forms when the waves reinforce.
A dark fringe forms when equal, opposite displacements cancel.
Destructive superposition gives a dark fringe, not a bright one.

parts.correctFeedback: A bright fringe forms when the waves reinforce.

options.feedback: Constructive superposition reinforces the waves, so the fringe is bright.
A bright fringe forms when the waves reinforce.
A dark fringe forms when equal, opposite displacements cancel.
Destructive superposition gives a dark fringe, not a bright one.

parts.correctFeedback: A dark fringe forms when equal, opposite displacements cancel.

questions.modelAnswer: (a) C: 1000/500 = 2λ. (b) B: a whole-number path difference makes the waves arrive in phase, giving constructive superposition and a bright fringe. (c) C: 750/500 = 1.5λ, an odd number of half-wavelengths. The waves arrive in antiphase; equal amplitudes cancel, giving a dark fringe.
generalFeedback: Divide path difference by wavelength: 1000 nm is two wavelengths.
Whole-number wavelength differences give in-phase arrival. Displacements add, producing a bright fringe.
Odd half-wavelength differences give antiphase arrival. Equal, opposite displacements cancel, producing a dark fringe.
questions.hint: Divide each path difference by 500 nm. Decide whether it is a whole number or an odd number of halves.
sources: SPEC A1.3; N24 Q5(b); J23 Q1(b). Double-slit representation selected in teacher feedback.
questions.accessibleDescription: Schematic with two narrow slits S1 and S2 and a screen on the right. Both paths to P and both paths to Q are shown. P has path difference 1000 nm; Q has path difference 750 nm; wavelength is 500 nm. Geometry is not to scale.

questions.title: Calculate string tension and pitch
questions.prompt: A string has wave speed 150 m/s and mass per unit length μ = 0.0020 kg/m. It is fixed at both ends, 0.50 m apart, and vibrates in its fundamental mode. Calculate its tension and fundamental frequency. Use v = √(T/μ) and v = fλ.

options.feedback: Square the speed, then multiply by mass per unit length.
The speed must be squared.
Multiply by μ after squaring.
This rearrangement reverses the required relationship.

parts.correctFeedback: Square the speed, then multiply by mass per unit length.
Your value is correct.
Your value is correct.
parts.incorrectFeedback: The length is half a wavelength, so double 0.50 m.

parts.correctFeedback: Your value is correct.
parts.incorrectFeedback: Divide 150 m/s by the wavelength in metres.

questions.modelAnswer: T = v²μ = 150² × 0.0020 = 45 N. The string contains half a wavelength, so λ = 2 × 0.50 = 1.0 m. f = v/λ = 150/1.0 = 150 Hz.
generalFeedback: T = vμ forgets to square the speed.
μ is mass per metre of string, not the total mass.
In the fundamental mode, L is half a wavelength, not a full wavelength.
questions.hint: Square both sides of the tension equation. For the second calculation, identify the fraction of a wavelength between the fixed ends.

questions.title: Apply the inverse-square law
questions.prompt: In an ideal model, a transmitter spreads its energy uniformly in all directions. Signal intensity is 0.072 W/m² at 3.0 m. Assume no absorption or obstacles. Calculate the intensity at 9.0 m. Use I = k/r².

parts.prompt: Calculate k from the first position.
parts.correctFeedback: Your value is correct.

options.feedback: Square the distance before dividing.
Increasing distance should reduce intensity.
9.0² = 81, so divide k by 81.
This reverses the inverse-square relationship.

parts.correctFeedback: 9.0² = 81, so divide k by 81.
Your value is correct.

questions.modelAnswer: k = 0.072 × 3.0² = 0.648 W. I = 0.648/9.0² = 0.648/81 = 0.0080 W/m². Tripling the distance reduces intensity by a factor of 9.
generalFeedback: Dividing by 9 instead of 81 misses the square on distance.
Intensity falls with distance under the stated model.
The ratio is (old distance/new distance)², so intensity becomes one ninth of its original value.
questions.hint: Find k from the first position. Square the second distance before dividing.

parts.prompt: Determine the periodic time from graph B.
parts.correctFeedback: Your value is correct.
parts.incorrectFeedback: Measure a crest-to-crest interval on the time axis.

questions.title: Compare methods: written self-assessment test
questions.prompt: A museum guide sends information to a nearby display. Visitors frequently walk between the devices. The table shows successful transmissions out of 12. Compare the methods, explain the effect of the obstruction and suggest the more suitable method for the museum. Write your answer before revealing the marking points.
questions.modelAnswer: Both methods worked in all 12 trials with a clear path. With an obstruction, infrared succeeded in 3/12 trials and Bluetooth in 11/12. The obstruction blocks much of the infrared signal, which needs a clear line of sight. Bluetooth uses radio waves that could pass through this obstruction well enough for reception. Bluetooth is the better choice here because visitors frequently interrupt the path and the obstructed results show greater reliability.
generalFeedback: Use both methods and the data in your comparison.
Explain why the signals behave differently, then relate your choice to this museum.
Enter the score you award yourself after checking the four points.

questions.title: Explain transmission in an optical fibre
questions.prompt: An optical fibre has core refractive index 1.50 and cladding refractive index 1.40. The critical angle at this boundary is 69°. A ray reaches the boundary from inside the core at an incidence angle of 75°. Explain how the light remains in the core. Complete the answer by selecting one sentence for each gap.

options.text: The core has a lower refractive index than the cladding.
options.feedback: 1.50 is greater than 1.40; the direction is reversed.

options.text: The core and cladding have equal refractive indices.
options.feedback: The supplied indices are different.

options.text: The core has a greater refractive index than the cladding.
options.feedback: Yes: light approaches the boundary from the higher-index material.

options.text: Light travels faster in the core than in the cladding.
options.feedback: A greater refractive index means a lower light speed.

parts.correctFeedback: Yes: light approaches the boundary from the higher-index material.

parts.prompt: Gap 2: Relate the incidence angle to the critical angle.

options.text: The incidence angle is greater than the critical angle at this boundary.
options.feedback: Yes: 75° exceeds the supplied critical angle of 69°.

options.text: The incidence angle must equal the critical angle at this boundary.
options.feedback: Equality would give a refracted ray along the boundary.

options.text: The incidence angle is less than the critical angle at this boundary.
options.feedback: 75° is greater than 69°, not less.

options.text: Any non-zero incidence angle is sufficient at this boundary.
options.feedback: The angle must exceed the critical angle, not merely exceed zero.

parts.correctFeedback: Yes: 75° exceeds the supplied critical angle of 69°.

parts.prompt: Gap 3: Explain how the light remains in the core.

options.text: Light refracts into the cladding and then reflects from the outer surface.
options.feedback: The required reflection is at the core-cladding boundary.

options.text: Light is absorbed by the core and re-emitted at each boundary.
options.feedback: Absorption and re-emission are not the TIR mechanism.

options.text: Light is totally internally reflected back into the core at successive boundaries.
options.feedback: Yes: repeated TIR keeps the ray in the core.

options.text: Light is reflected because it approaches the boundary from the lower-index material.
options.feedback: The light approaches from the higher-index core.

parts.correctFeedback: Yes: repeated TIR keeps the ray in the core.

questions.modelAnswer: The ray reaches the core-cladding boundary from inside the core. The core has a greater refractive index than the cladding. The incidence angle is greater than the critical angle at this boundary. Light is totally internally reflected back into the core at successive boundaries.
generalFeedback: Both TIR conditions are needed: higher-to-lower refractive index and incidence above the critical angle.
The supplied opening sentence earns no marks. Each missing explanation point is marked independently.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by refraction. Select one answer.

options.text: A change in direction when a wave changes speed on crossing a boundary at an angle.

options.text: A wave returning into the original medium after meeting a boundary.

options.text: Waves spreading when they pass through an aperture or past an edge.

options.text: A wave losing energy as it travels through a material.
